title: Russia: society under strain, an economy on a war footing
label: 20 October 2026 · Russia
summary: Two panels of experts described a Russia that is increasingly militarised and repressive, socially strained by a prolonged war in Ukraine, and economically squeezed by debt, falling energy revenues and sanctions. The speakers agreed the system is resilient but brittle: Putin’s centralised rule holds so long as elites feel it can win, while the economy is being sustained by costly credit and diverted energy flows that Western sanctions and Ukrainian attacks are progressively degrading. The witnesses identified leverage points—better enforcement of existing sanctions, maritime insurance controls and targeting of refining loopholes—that the UK and partners could use to increase pressure.

chapters.title: How life in Russia feels now
chapters.takeaway: Daily life looked fairly normal in big cities until this year, but Ukrainian strikes, inflation and tax hikes have made life noticeably harder for ordinary Russians.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Paint for us what Russia is like now for ordinary people — has it changed recently?

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: In big cities until recently people still shopped and ate out, despite sanctions. But this year is different: Ukrainian strikes have reached oil refineries and large firms, leading to shop and restaurant closures and real pain in household budgets.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: The Kremlin used cash incentives to recruit fighters, so many volunteered for pay. Now, after months of strikes and tax hikes, polls show growing pessimism — two-thirds in one August poll thought things would get worse.

turns.speaker: Dr Ruth Deyermond
turns.text: Putin's rule has lasted 25 years: two generations have grown up under increasingly authoritarian government. The 1990s were more pluralistic, but that window has long closed.

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: Socially, there is a familiar posture of confrontation toward the west. Repression is severe: people can face long jail terms over small acts of dissent. Many Russians have fallen into line with state narratives.

chapters.title: Putinism: ideology and resilience
chapters.takeaway: Putinism presents a coherent worldview—Russia as a historic great power defending itself from a hostile west—which helps bind elites and society, making the regime resilient though brittle.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How resilient is Putin's regime and is 'Putinism' an ideology or just state practice?

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: It's resilient. The ideology says Russia has a distinctive place, is mistreated by the west, and deserves a zone of influence near its borders. That worldview unites the ruling class and justifies centralised, autocratic rule.

turns.speaker: Dr Ruth Deyermond
turns.text: Putinism draws on an older belief that Russia must be a great power to survive. That idea is central to elites' thinking: the west is seen as an existential threat, making rapprochement unlikely without regime change.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: The elite mostly backed the war; some were surprised by the scale. Their support depends on whether they think the Kremlin is winning. If western unity falters, elites breathe easier; recent disinformation and political shifts in Europe worry them.

chapters.title: Opposition, elites and succession
chapters.takeaway: There is no organised popular opposition able to topple the regime; political change is likelier to come from elite splits, but the forms that could take are uncertain.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is there a groundswell against Putin, or is the opposition simply crushed and fragmented?

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: Society is atomised by repression, so change is unlikely to come from mass protests. Historically, elites drive regime change in Russia; if that happens, it may be sudden and messy.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: We have seen elite infighting at times of stress. A technocratic faction around Sergey Kiriyenko wants a more pragmatic relationship with the west and is building political platforms, but they only act when they think Putin is losing.

turns.speaker: Dr Ruth Deyermond
turns.text: Because the state has been re-geared for war—education, law enforcement, the penal system—any real change in direction will probably require a change of regime type, not just personality changes.

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: The Wagner mutiny showed a precedent for internal armed challenge. If Putin weakens—through health or political problems—collective leadership struggles could follow, as in Soviet history.

chapters.title: Repression, media and social consequences
chapters.takeaway: The state tightly controls information and punishes dissent; manipulation of narratives abroad and media restrictions at home deepen isolation and hinder opposition.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How tightly can the Russian state control information, and what can the west do to reach Russians with independent news?

turns.speaker: Dr Ruth Deyermond
turns.text: Russia has restricted internet access and criminalised dissent. Western broadcasters still matter—BBC World Service and others are vital—but practical workarounds and technical means are needed to increase reach inside Russia.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: Kremlin disinformation is a major front of the war—co-ordinated, well-resourced campaigns aim to undermine western support for Ukraine. It adapts to social media and uses proxies in Europe.

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: There is a deep conspiratorial view of the west in parts of Russian society. That view is reinforced by state media and mirrored by Russian reports that try to discredit western human rights claims.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does exposing corruption in the elite change Russian public opinion?

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: Corruption at the top is widely expected; people are more affected by prices and living standards than elite graft. Corruption matters politically only when the war looks like a long, losing drag on the economy.

chapters.title: The economy: militarisation, credit and debt
chapters.takeaway: Russia has a militarised economy funded by high-cost credit, depleted savings and punitive taxation; this creates a growing debt problem that risks a financial crisis.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is Russia's economy collapsing, holding up or in-between? Is it a full war economy?

turns.speaker: Dr Nigel Gould-Davies
turns.text: Russia is increasingly militarised but not a classical war economy: it avoids mass compulsory mobilisation and instead pays high incentives. That makes the war very expensive and inequitable.

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: Russia engineered a credit boom after 2022 that turned into a bubble. They spent down the national welfare fund and added lots of corporate debt to sustain growth and the war. Now investment is dropping and stress is rising.

turns.speaker: Dr Nigel Gould-Davies
turns.text: Next year's draft budget plans a big rise in defence spending—nominally around 40%—but that will be paid for by cuts elsewhere, higher taxes and more domestic borrowing. The fund is nearly empty.

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: Russia's borrowing costs are high: 10-year yields are near 17% domestically. The state pays more debt servicing relative to its economy than Germany; that indicates a heavy annual burden despite a low debt-to-GDP headline.

turns.speaker: Dr Nigel Gould-Davies
turns.text: The regions are strained too. Local budgets have run deficits after being obliged to help pay recruitment bonuses. Those regional shortfalls are implicit federal liabilities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How sustainable is this model if they keep paying big bonuses rather than mobilising?

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: It can be maintained only short-term. The more they rely on expensive credits and subsidies, the higher the risk of cascading defaults or a credit event that forces painful adjustments.

chapters.title: Energy, sanctions and where the UK can press harder
chapters.takeaway: Sanctions and Ukrainian strikes have cut Russia's energy earnings; the UK and EU retain important leverage—maritime insurance, enforcement of the price cap and closing refining and shadow-fleet loopholes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How have sanctions and Ukrainian strikes affected Russia's oil and gas, and what practical levers remain?

turns.speaker: Isaac Levi
turns.text: Oil and gas taxes once funded a third to half of the budget. In early 2026 that fell to about 18% of state revenue; refining capacity is down—estimates say 30–50% lost to strikes—and diesel shortages followed.

turns.speaker: Isaac Levi
turns.text: Russia still exports volumes but at heavy discounts to buyers in India, China and Turkey, lowering export earnings. The 'shadow fleet' and false flags help move oil, and UK maritime insurers still cover a lot of Russian coal and LNG shipments.

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: The UK has exceptional leverage through maritime insurance and the global trading infrastructure based in London. Prudently used, insurance controls and targeted sanctions can close loopholes and deepen the price squeeze.

turns.speaker: Dr Nigel Gould-Davies
turns.text: Enforcement matters: the oil price-cap is violated by attestation fraud; better verification and pressure on the shadow fleet, plus coordinated action with Europe and the US, would amplify impact.

turns.speaker: Isaac Levi
turns.text: Specific options: tighten verification of price-cap attestation, sanction or tax use of UK insurance for vessels serving the shadow fleet, ban imports of refined products made from Russian crude, and target false flag registries.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If US policy softens, would that undercut these measures?

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: The UK and EU dominate maritime insurance and have meaningful unilateral levers. US moves matter on dollar finance, but London remains the key place to act on shipping and insurance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final brief point on what matters most now?

turns.speaker: Dr Nigel Gould-Davies
turns.text: Use what works: enforce existing sanctions, close refining and shipping loopholes, coordinate on China policy as it enables some flows, and consider ways to mobilise frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine.
